title: Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In residential construction, profitability is won or lost in the procurement of steel and aluminum formwork, but solvency is decided in the velocity of channel-partner collections.
epigraph.author: Nitin Bavisi, Chief Financial Officer, Investor Earnings Concall

web_blocks.text: The distribution and go-to-market architecture of Mumbai real estate has undergone a profound professionalization over the past decade. Historically reliant on localized, informal property brokers operating out of neighborhood storefronts. Ajmera Realty today operates an omnichannel sales engine combining an in-house institutional sales force. Institutional International Property Consultants (IPCs) such as JLL, CBRE, Knight Frank. Anarock, an extensive network of accredited Channel Partners (CPs). Digital pre-sales funnels targeting non-resident Indian (NRI) buyers across the Middle East. United Kingdom, and North America. [2][4][6]

Channel partners form the primary frontline distribution pipeline for high-velocity residential launches. In major Mumbai suburban micro-markets. Accredited CPs account for approximately 65% to 75% of initial launch bookings. Ajmera’s direct corporate sales and digital inquiry desk capturing the remaining 25% to 35%. Brokerage commissions are tightly structured: standard CP commissions range between 2.0% and 3.5% of agreement value. Stepped incentive ladders triggered when a distributor achieves predefined sales quotas (e.g.. Selling 20 or more units during a launch campaign). To prevent speculative channel hoarding and artificial booking spikes. Ajmera enforces strict validation: commission tranches are only disbursed to channel partners after the customer has executed a registered agreement for sale and cleared a minimum 10% to 20% down payment. [4][6][8]

The supply chain and civil engineering execution footprint relies on established engineering contractors and specialized subcontractors. Rather than carrying heavy in-house labor payrolls across boom-and-bust cycles. Ajmera engages tier-1 and tier-2 civil engineering contracting firms for structural core-and-shell execution. The company standardizes its high-rise residential construction on Mivan aluminum formwork systems—a modular. Reusable shuttering technology that replaces traditional timber scaffolding and brick masonry with monolithic reinforced concrete. While Mivan shuttering demands higher upfront capital investment for tooling and fabrication. It compresses floor-to-floor cycle times from 21 days down to 8 to 10 days. Delivering superior structural seismic tolerance, smoother surface finishes, and zero brickwork plastering requirements. [2][4]

Procurement of raw materials—predominantly Thermo-Mechanically Treated (TMT) steel rebar. Portland Pozzolana Cement (PPC), Ready-Mix Concrete (RMC). Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) infrastructure—is managed through centralized group contracts. By pooling material demand across Wadala high-rises and suburban redevelopment sites. Management negotiates volume price discounts directly with primary producers including Tata Steel, JSW Steel. UltraTech Cement, insulating project budgets from retail building-material inflation. Civil contracts typically incorporate price escalation adjustment bands: if structural steel or cement prices swing beyond a 5% to 10% threshold. Cost variances are shared between developer and contractor according to index-linked CPWD escalation formulas. [2][4][6]

web_blocks.region_era: Mumbai, Slum Rehabilitation & Suburban Land Banking, 2008–2018
web_blocks.mechanism: A high-profile Mumbai developer accumulated massive land-development rights and took on aggressive construction debt across ambitious SRA projects (including the Mumbai Airport Slum Rehabilitation project). When regulatory approvals were delayed and pre-sales collections lagged rising debt service costs, working capital froze, interest compounded, and the business entered terminal insolvency.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: HDIL collapsed from annual revenues exceeding ₹1,800 crore and a peak market capitalization of over ₹15,000 crore in 2008 to defaulting on over ₹8,000 crore in debt, resulting in NCLT corporate insolvency proceedings in 2019.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: For Ajmera, HDIL represents the definitive failure base rate of Mumbai development: taking on aggressive upfront debt for complex land rights without matched milestone cash collections will bankrupt even a developer with vast urban holdings. Ajmera's structural shift to asset-light redevelopment and debt reduction to 0.44x is a mandatory safeguard against this exact trap.

web_blocks.text: The billing, collection, and cash-flow recognition cycle is governed by strict RERA milestone schedules. Unlike manufacturing or software enterprises that recognize revenue upon invoice generation. Indian residential developers recognize revenue only when projects cross defined percentage-of-completion hurdles and units qualify for customer handover under Ind AS 115. Collections, however, follow physical construction progress. Under standard construction-linked payment plans (CLPs). A typical 100% agreement value is collected across ten discrete milestone gates: 10% on booking, 10% on agreement registration. 15% upon completion of plinth, 25% distributed across intermediate floor slabs. 15% upon completion of walls and internal plastering, 15% upon external finishing and MEP installation. The final 10% upon receipt of the municipal Occupation Certificate (OC) and physical key handover. [4][6][8]

web_blocks.caption: Table 3.1: Ajmera Realty Worked ₹100 Revenue-to-Free-Cash-Flow Waterfall (Audited FY26)
web_blocks.takeaway: In FY26, of every ₹100 in billed revenue, ₹63.49 was absorbed by direct construction materials and municipal FSI premiums, ₹3.49 funded payroll, and ₹5.69 covered marketing and overhead, leaving an Operating EBITDA of ₹27.34. After debt interest (-₹6.70) and taxes (-₹6.61), reported PAT was ₹14.40. Working-capital reinvestment in active construction lowered operating cash conversion to ₹6.33 per ₹100 of revenue.

web_blocks.text: The worked ₹100 waterfall provides critical forensic insight into the unit economics of Mumbai development. While the accounting margin appears strong—EBITDA at 27.34% and PAT at 14.40%—the actual cash conversion reveals the capital intensity of high-rise construction. Out of ₹100 in billed revenue, only ₹6.33 converted into operating cash flow in FY26. Net free cash flow standing at ₹3.67 after project-level capex. This divergence occurs because Ajmera was actively pouring capital into excavation, piling. Podium construction for Ajmera Manhattan 2 and Ajmera Solis. In high-rise real estate, cash outflows precede customer milestone billings by six to twelve months. Once towers pass the intermediate slab stage, customer milestone billings accelerate. This expanded cash conversion. [1][6][8]

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand why real estate development is so frequently misunderstood by public equity markets, you have to follow the cash through the physical supply chain. In an ordinary manufacturing business, you buy raw steel on thirty-day credit, stamp it into components over three days. Collect from your customer thirty days later. The entire working-capital cycle resolves in two months. In urban high-rise construction, the developer lives in an entirely different financial universe: you commit capital to municipal premiums and excavation today. Your final cash realization arrives four years later when the municipal building inspector signs the Occupation Certificate.

Consider the distribution network that must be mobilized to fill a forty-storey tower like Ajmera Manhattan. Management does not simply wait for walk-in buyers to wander into a sales gallery. They activate hundreds of independent channel partners across Mumbai, arming them with virtual reality walkthroughs, detailed floor plans, and calibrated commission tiers. These channel partners are aggressive and highly mobile. They will steer an affluent buyer toward whichever developer offers the smoothest transaction experience and the most reliable delivery record. By enforcing strict registration and down-payment rules before paying brokerage fees, Ajmera protects itself from the speculative churn that burned so many builders in previous cycles.

On the construction site, the choice of building technology is a profound economic decision. Walking through an Ajmera high-rise under construction, you will not see masons laying red clay bricks by hand with trowels. You see massive modular panels of Mivan aluminum formwork bolted together to form the entire floor plate—walls, columns, and ceilings simultaneously. High-strength concrete is pumped forty storeys straight up into the molds in a single continuous pour. When the aluminum panels are stripped down forty-eight hours later, the concrete structure is completely cured and atomically smooth. This industrialization cuts floor cycle times by half, saving tens of crores in capitalized interest.

Now study our worked one-hundred-rupee waterfall, because it reveals the central tension in Ajmera's financial profile. On an accounting basis, the business looks extraordinarily profitable: for every hundred rupees of revenue, twenty-seven rupees flow to operating profit and over fourteen rupees reach the net profit line. But when you look at the cash line, only six rupees and thirty-three paise survived as operating cash flow in FY26. Where did the rest go? It was absorbed into working capital: pouring concrete for towers that have been pre-sold but cannot yet be recognized on the P&L, paying transit rent for redevelopment societies, and funding contractor mobilization advances.

This is why the cautionary tale of HDIL must be etched into our minds. A decade ago, HDIL sat on massive development rights in Mumbai and reported hundreds of crores in paper profits. But its management borrowed recklessly to acquire more slum rehabilitation rights while failing to convert active construction into realized customer cash collections. When the credit window slammed shut, the interest burden devoured the equity. Ajmera's financial survival depends on ensuring that every rupee deployed into concrete at Wadala or Vikhroli is backed by enforceable, escrowed customer collection milestones.

You and I must also examine the human element of high-rise construction logistics in Mumbai. A 45-storey tower is not just an engineering feat. It is a complex choreographed ballet of hundreds of skilled laborers, heavy tower cranes, concrete boom placers, and municipal safety inspectors. During the four months of the monsoon season—from June through September—torrential rains flood excavation pits and halt external plastering. During major festive periods like Diwali, construction workers travel back to their ancestral villages across Uttar Pradesh, Bihar. West Bengal for weeks at a time. A developer that fails to anticipate these seasonal labor migrations will face costly schedule slippages.

Ajmera navigates these seasonal bottlenecks through disciplined procurement scheduling. Heavy foundation excavation and basement raft casting are completed during the dry winter and spring months. During the monsoon, labor is deployed internally to complete electrical conduit laying, plumbing rough-ins. Drywall installation within already-cured lower floors. By utilizing Mivan aluminum shuttering, the company minimizes reliance on traditional masonry plasterers. This ensures that structural concrete progress continues at a steady pace regardless of weather friction.

Consider also the governance of RERA escrow accounts. Before RERA, a developer could collect twenty crore rupees from buyers in Wadala and immediately wire that cash to an unzoned land seller in Panvel. Today, the municipal architect, the chartered accountant. The structural engineer must independently certify the exact percentage of physical completion before the escrow bank releases a single rupee. This regulatory ring-fencing introduces administrative friction. For you and me as equity analysts, it provides an invaluable institutional guarantee: customer advances cannot be diverted into speculative vanity projects.

When you observe the physical execution of these towers from ground excavation to high-rise topping out, you appreciate the immense technical coordination required to deliver high-quality urban housing. Every cubic meter of ready-mix concrete must be tested for compressive strength, every bundle of steel rebar must undergo tensile yield testing. Every plumbing riser must pass pressure checks before walls are sealed. By institutionalizing these quality control workflows and standardizing on aluminum formwork, Ajmera protects its brand reputation and ensures that home buyers receive homes that endure for generations.
Our underwriting reflects these physical facts. Construction execution requires steady operational vigilance across every concrete pour.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The worked waterfall illustrates the fundamental paradox of real estate accounting: high accounting profits can mask weak immediate cash conversion during heavy launch years. As long as Ajmera maintains its 0.44x debt-to-equity discipline and collects 70% of buyer payments into escrow, this working capital reinvestment builds future revenue visibility; if collections falter, however, that inventory quickly becomes a balance-sheet drag.
